Free Will, Mind Body Dualism and Stupidity with Prager University

While there are problems with the topic itself, Prager University is presenting a standard understanding of cognitivism. If the brain is just a complicated mechanism that takes an input and produces an output, then there is nothing to say about "free will", everything is just a stimulus and a response - but that is behaviorism which cognitivism violently rejects, so there must be something else going on, perhaps a "mind" which can have representations and have thoughts and make decisions. This is where the Rational Channel stops listening, which is funny because they have already planted themselves firmly in the neurological behaviorism camp (thoughts are caused by "environmental stimulus and neurochemistry" [at 00:50]). TRC: The mind is the brain, you are your brain, all we have to do is understand neurochemistry a little better and we can reduce everyone to a... Prager: machine that doesn't really have free will at all. But again, cognitivism rejects this, which is why they move to a mind / body dualism. TRC then becomes petulant, "prove it, prove there is a meta-brain! You have no evidence!"

Early in the video TRC explains that getting nervous about giving a lecture is caused by the external event of the lecture acting on the brain, and thinking about this representation of the lecture causes the person to get nervous. But how can you say there is an external cause if the lecture has not occurred, is still in the future? If the lecture is cancelled (the auditorium burns down the day before) then person has been stimulated by something nonexistent, so what stimulated the brain? Perhaps a past experience of giving a lecture, or stories from other people about how they got nervous giving lectures. Then how did those external events get into the brain? If the experience happened to you, then it is part of your history, easy enough. And if the experience was artificially implanted into your brain, that should also be acceptable (if you are TRC). The experiences of others requires their stories to become somehow represented in the brain, like an implant but without all the surgery. But then if other people's nervous experiences can get put into your brain, and you are told you have to give a lecture on Friday, then you have no control of your thinking, you will become nervous - unless there is some other mechanism that prevents you from becoming nervous, some other part of the brain that provides confidence. But how is it that a part of the brain is isolated from the part of your brain that listens to stories about getting nervous over lectures, so that your confidence will prevent you from getting nervous? It requires a lot of speculation about certain structures in the brain, to which I say: "Prove it, prove those structures exist. You have no evidence!"

It doesn't matter if the presentation gets cancelled. If someone threatens to beat you up which increases stress and you get the internal response and then that person says they were just joking the stimulus (external) was still perceived as real at the time regardless of whether it was actually real or gets cancelled. The point of the example was to outline that internal and external is a poor choice of terminology due to how messy the topic is.
If you can prove that two current models don't work you don't get to just move on to mid body dualism, they didn't outline that neurochemistry being the base for the "mind" doesn't work and even if they did that doesn't make mind body dualism true. They would have to actually prove mind body dualism.
Regarding your claim of different structures in the brain regarding confidence I think you have taken something from the video that wasn't there or not intended, You may have to elaborate there.

The video presents thoughts in the form of "environmental stimulus and neurochemistry" as a good model, but the cognitivists have already rejected previous forms of behaviorism and would reject neurological behaviorism as well - this dates back to arguments between Skinner and Chomsky in the 50's, which the cognitivists claim to have won. I'm not saying I believe in this victory or that mind / body dualism is a good model, but this dualism is a pretty fundamental concept for certain disciplines. It doesn't really rise to the level of god or God or GOD but it isn't incompatible with theism, either.

As for a model of neurological structures and how external stimulus becomes an internal stimulus producing a response, I am simply sketching out the way that any theory proposing a "black box" mechanism for taking observable stimuli and producing observable responses is going to require fairly elaborate hypotheses to explain how the black box works... and - given the positivist origins of behaviorism - those hypotheses will have to be shown to be true, or at least evidence will have to point towards their validity. This is quite a difficult position to be in, even for the neurochemist with access to an MRI, because the internal representations of events or thoughts or ideas will have to be demonstrated to occur within the brain in order to satisfy the theory. In other words, if you want to show me a number of ways that external events can produce stress and result in an increased heart rate etc, you have to show the way that the external event matches the pattern of some member of the set of stimuli that cause stress, and that the internal stimulus of stress produces the response of an increased heart rate etc on a neurological level. That should be easy to do, yet we are still fumbling around with the ways that optical nerves stimulate pattern centers in the brain, and a more abstract internal stimulus ("this causes stress") is very difficult to quantify. And if that stimulus can be a either a real external stimulus or an internal stimulus caused by imaginary events, how much evidence, from how many subjects, will we need to be satisfied with this conclusion?

The video itself is addressing a lack of evidence in Prager's claims and merely suggests that when we follow the evidence to a conclusion rather than begin with the conclusion then we arrive at a consciousness which is derived from physical structures. All the evidence has shown that cognition is dependent / influenced / controlled / or a result of physical components.

Behaviourism no longer has much to do with psychology, you are referring to a debate between cognitivism and behaviourism which is out-dated to say the least. These two things are philosophical perspectives of Psychology and psychology is not a hard science. We now have the technology to measure and quantify behaviour and cognition. Neuroscience now plays a greater role in psychology than previous methods of behavioural studies and though it is a relatively new methodology for behavioural science (because the technology is new) it is has produced some amazing results. Just jump on Google scholar if you don't already have access to a scholarly database and you will see what I'm talking about.

Neuroscience is following the same positivist program that behaviorism was following nearly 80 years ago, which you demonstrate every time you mention (or demand) "evidence". But you aren't going to persuade anyone on the cognitivism side of the debate to agree with you until you resolve the philosophical divide between the camps. They will look at your neural structures and say, "Yes, you have created a model of a brain taking input and producing output, but we are looking for the way the mind handles representations." It doesn't help that the other big success in psychology is cognitive behavior therapy, which is both badly named and a fairly direct result of the behaviorist research program that was thought to have been defeated in the 1950's. It is a tough time to be a cognitivist.

But that is a sideline to the philosophical question of what happens when someone becomes nervous due to an event that has not yet occurred, how does your neuroscience answer the question of what is causing the nervousness? Perhaps it is the unfamiliarity of the experience, a lack of a known pattern to act as an input, and "nervousness" has somehow come to be the conditioned response (replacing the crying response of an infant and the disregard by a teenager) which can be shown neurologically. But I don't think that will be a satisfactory answer, this might be the correct cause of the response for person A, where we can follow their history and determine how the neural patterns formed over time and those patterns produce nervousness in this situation, but what about person B for whom lectures are a commonplace event yet they still get nervous? You have to map out all of these individual histories which are of endless variety, yet somehow connect each individual history with a general idea of "nervousness". But wait, you have actually lost your grasp on what it means to be nervous, since all of these unique histories produce unique responses that are only understood to be "nervousness" by some convention of similarity. Getting nervous is simply the set of responses which you classify as nervousness, a very limited set, and that set is always going to be smaller that the set of responses which you have yet to categorize. The program of neuroscience can only examine a limited number of responses, but you want it to explain that all thoughts are the result of environmental stimulus and neurochemisty. Positivism can't do this, because positivism can only explain empirical phenomena that can be measured. Some thoughts can be measured, but are those thoughts the totality of all possible thoughts?

The hardware I'm talking about is laptop, but as you know, the word laptop is an abstraction that hides tons of things such as a Graphics card, Wifi adaptor, Ethernet controller, PCI controller, Touchpad, USB slots, USB Modem (external accessory), etc. etc.

What I'm looking for?

Does the Linux community maintain a mapping for hardware drivers for each of these equipment against its compatibility for each Distro? Something like this (for example):

Broadcom Wireless LAN Adapter 7197

Ubuntu: Yes LinuxMint: Yes Fedora: Yes Debian: No

Why is it useful?

You see, all Linux users are not pros and full-time expert in one thing. If I'm looking to buy a new laptop, the first thing I'll do is visit Amazon.com and compare prices. Out of the 100 different branded models (like Dell Inspiron, Toshiba Satellite, Asus, Samsung, etc.), the only things I can practically filter out are price and specs (CPU/RAM/HDD/GraphicCard). If I start researching the internals, each laptop can have at least ten different internal components like Synaptic Touchpad, Wifi & LAN cards, etc. that can have compatibility issues. So the combination works out to be like (100 * 20 = 2000). Neither do I have time for doing such detailed analysis, nor I'm sure that anything could be even found.

If I take the adventurous route of first buying the cheapest laptop and then if compatibility breaks, come here on /r/linux and ask for help like many other folks, its a futile and time-consuming exercise and the answer in most cases is: This firmware vendor doesn't support linux.

tldr; In short, do we maintain such a database or not and whether do we think such a database is useful for us? I think that maintaining such a database is helpful as on one hand, it won't force lots of us noobs to stick to Ubuntu or just keep replacing our hardware. On the other hand, if each noob started looking up this database before shopping for their hardware, the vendors not supporting (or poorly supporting) linux will gradually loose a portion of the market which is a big victory for the Linux community. Yes. Look into something called PGP. You make a private key and a public key. You give people you want to be able to decrypt your messages the public key. You put a password on the private key and give it to nobody. Then you collect public keys from people you want to be able to talk to. Then you type whatever you want in a program that supports it, I use pgp4USB, and then encrypt it with the public key of whoever you are talking to. Then they take your encrypted message and put it in a program that has their private key stored in it and they decrypt it with that, which requires their password. The same thing applies to you when they give you messages encrypted with your key. The only way to read messages ebcrypted with public keys is to have the corresponding private key that belongs to it.
